severity_estimate: Moderate to High (Progressive condition; can lead to severe vision impairment or blindness if untreated)
possible_causes: Natural aging process (most common cause of protein aggregation in the lens)
Long-term exposure to ultraviolet (UV) sunlight without protection
Systemic health conditions such as Diabetes Mellitus
Ocular trauma or prior eye surgery
common_symptoms: Cloudy, blurry, foggy, or dim vision
Increased sensitivity to light and glare, especially while driving at night
Frequent changes in eyeglass or contact lens prescriptions
Double vision in a single eye (monocular diplopia)
treatment_suggestions: Early stages: Prescription update, anti-glare lens coatings, magnifying lenses, and brighter lighting
Definitive treatment: Cataract surgery (phacoemulsification) to remove the cloudy lens and replace it with an artificial Intraocular Lens (IOL)
Note: Eye drops or medications cannot reverse or stop cataract progression
prevention_tips: Wear sunglasses with 100% UV protection (UVA/UVB) outdoors
Maintain strict control of blood sugar levels if diabetic
Quit smoking and limit alcohol intake
Eat a diet rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and vitamin E (e.g., leafy greens)
Schedule regular comprehensive dilated eye exams
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult an ophthalmologist if you experience progressive cloudy or blurry vision, increased glare at night, or frequent prescription changes. Seek urgent medical attention if you experience sudden vision loss, severe eye pain, or flashes of light.

possible_causes: N/A - Normal anatomical and physiological ocular health without evidence of pathology
common_symptoms: Clear, sharp vision at distance and near (with or without corrective lenses)
Clear, transparent cornea and crystalline lens
Moist, comfortable eyes without pain, dryness, or excessive tearing
Normal tear film quality and healthy pink conjunctiva
Unrestricted visual field and normal intraocular pressure
treatment_suggestions: No medical or surgical treatment required
Maintain routine preventive eye care and eye safety practices
prevention_tips: Follow the 20-20-20 rule during screen use (look 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes)
Wear protective safety glasses during sports, woodworking, or high-risk activities
Use UV-blocking sunglasses in bright sunlight
Practice proper contact lens hygiene (never sleep in lenses unless prescribed)
Eat a nutrient-dense diet supporting eye health (omega-3 fatty acids, lutein, zinc)
when_to_see_a_doctor: Schedule routine comprehensive eye exams every 1 to 2 years. See an eye doctor immediately if you notice sudden vision changes, eye injury, severe pain, persistent redness, or new floaters/flashes.

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Benign growth; can cause astigmatism or obscure vision if it invades the central cornea)
possible_causes: Chronic, unprotected exposure to high levels of ultraviolet (UV) radiation
Prolonged exposure to dry, dusty, windy, or sandy outdoor environments
Chronic eye irritation from environmental pollutants
Occupational factors (e.g., outdoor workers, farmers, surfers)
common_symptoms: Fleshy, pinkish, triangular growth on the conjunctiva extending onto the cornea
Localized eye redness, swelling, and chronic inflammation
Gritty, burning, or foreign-body sensation in the eye
Dryness and tearing due to disruption of the tear film
Blurred vision or astigmatism if the lesion grows large enough to distort corneal curvature
treatment_suggestions: Mild cases: Lubricating artificial tears and gel drops to soothe irritation
Short-term topical anti-inflammatory drops (e.g., mild steroids) for acute flare-ups under medical supervision
Surgical intervention: Surgical excision with conjunctival autografting or amniotic membrane graft if vision is affected or severe discomfort persists
prevention_tips: Wear wrap-around sunglasses with 100% UV protection to shield eyes from sun, wind, and dust
Wear wide-brimmed hats when spending extended periods outdoors
Use lubricating eye drops in dry, dusty, or arid environments to prevent chronic irritation
Avoid rubbing eyes when exposed to dust or sand
when_to_see_a_doctor: Schedule an eye evaluation if you notice a growing tissue mass on the surface of your eye, persistent redness/irritation, or if the growth alters your vision or visual field.
